description: Curated lay + clinical medical vocabulary used by MedChat AI's terminology recognizer. Each concept has a canonical id, a category, surface forms (synonyms and lay phrasings), abbreviations, and a plain-language definition shown in the UI.

concepts.definition: Blood pressure that stays higher than normal over time, which strains the heart and blood vessels.
Blood pressure lower than normal, which can cause dizziness or fainting.
A long-term condition where the body does not use insulin well, so blood sugar runs high.
An autoimmune condition where the pancreas makes little or no insulin.
A group of conditions in which blood sugar (glucose) levels are too high.
Blood sugar higher than normal but not yet in the diabetes range.
Blood sugar that drops below normal, causing shakiness, sweating, or confusion.
A chronic condition where the airways narrow and swell, making breathing difficult.
A long-term lung disease that blocks airflow and makes breathing harder.
An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs.
Inflammation of the airways that carry air to the lungs, often with a cough.
A contagious viral infection of the nose, throat, and lungs.
A respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
A mild viral infection of the nose and throat.
Inflammation or infection of the sinuses.
A bacterial throat infection that causes a sore, scratchy throat.
Damage to heart muscle when its blood supply is blocked.
Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart with blood.
A condition where the heart cannot pump blood as well as the body needs.
An irregular, often rapid heart rhythm that can raise stroke risk.
A heartbeat that is too fast, too slow, or irregular.
Damage to the brain from interrupted blood flow or bleeding.
A brief stroke-like episode that resolves but signals higher stroke risk.
Higher than healthy levels of fats such as cholesterol in the blood.
Not enough healthy red blood cells to carry adequate oxygen.
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg.
A blood clot that travels to and blocks an artery in the lungs.
Stomach acid flowing back into the esophagus, often causing heartburn.
A common gut disorder causing cramping, bloating, and changes in bowel habits.
Chronic inflammation of the digestive tract, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
Inflammation of the appendix, usually needing urgent treatment.
Inflammation of the stomach and intestines, causing vomiting and diarrhea.
A sore in the lining of the stomach or upper small intestine.
Hardened deposits that form in the gallbladder.
Hard mineral deposits that form in the kidneys.
Gradual loss of kidney function over time.
An infection in any part of the urinary system, most often the bladder.
The thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormone.
The thyroid gland makes too much thyroid hormone.
Breakdown of joint cartilage causing pain and stiffness.
An autoimmune disease that inflames the joints.
Inflammation of one or more joints, causing pain and stiffness.
Bones become weak and brittle, raising fracture risk.
A form of arthritis caused by uric acid crystals in a joint.
A break in a bone.
A stretched or torn ligament.
Inflammation or irritation of a tendon.
A spinal disc whose soft center pushes out and can press on nerves.
Pain along the sciatic nerve, from the lower back down the leg.
Recurring, often severe headaches, sometimes with nausea or light sensitivity.
A brain condition that causes recurring seizures.
A mild brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head.
A decline in memory and thinking severe enough to affect daily life.
A progressive nervous system disorder that affects movement.
A disease in which the immune system attacks the protective covering of nerves.
A mood disorder causing persistent sadness and loss of interest.
Ongoing worry or fear that interferes with daily activities.
Persistent trouble falling or staying asleep.
Breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep.
Excess body fat that increases the risk of other health problems.
A condition that makes skin red, dry, and itchy.
An immune condition causing scaly, inflamed patches of skin.
A painful rash caused by reactivation of the chickenpox virus.
A bacterial infection of the deeper layers of skin.
An immune reaction to a substance that is usually harmless.
A severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
Disease in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and can spread.
Inflammation of the clear membrane covering the white of the eye.
An infection of the middle ear.
The body loses more fluid than it takes in.
Discomfort in the chest; can be serious and may need urgent evaluation.
Feeling that you cannot get enough air.
Pain in any region of the head.
A body temperature higher than normal, often a sign of infection.
Feeling cold with shivering, often alongside fever.
A reflex that clears the airways of mucus or irritants.
Pain or irritation in the throat.
A blocked or runny nose.
A whistling sound when breathing, from narrowed airways.
An uneasy feeling in the stomach with an urge to vomit.
Forcefully bringing up stomach contents through the mouth.
Loose, watery bowel movements.
Infrequent or difficult bowel movements.
Pain felt anywhere between the chest and the groin.
A burning feeling in the chest, often from stomach acid.
A feeling of fullness or swelling in the belly.
Visible or dark blood in bowel movements; should be evaluated by a clinician.
Feeling faint, unsteady, or as if the room is spinning.
A brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.
Persistent tiredness or lack of energy.
Feeling that the heart is racing, pounding, or skipping beats.
Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the body's tissues.
An area of irritated or swollen skin, often red and itchy.
An irritating sensation that makes you want to scratch.
Pain felt in the back, most often the lower back.
Discomfort, aches, or soreness in a joint.
Aches or pain in the muscles.
Reduced feeling or a tingling sensation, often in hands or feet.
Reduced strength in one or more muscles.
Difficulty thinking clearly or knowing where you are.
Lack of sharpness in eyesight.
Needing to urinate more often than usual.
Pain or burning while urinating.
Feeling unusually thirsty.
A drop in body weight; unexplained loss should be checked by a clinician.
Heavy sweating during sleep.
Reduced or absent ability to smell or taste.
A pain reliever and fever reducer; too much can damage the liver.
A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) for pain, fever, and inflammation.
A longer-acting NSAID used for pain and inflammation.
An NSAID used for pain and, at low doses, to reduce clotting.
A class of pain relievers that reduce inflammation, such as ibuprofen and naproxen.
A first-line medicine that lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.
A hormone, given as medicine, that lowers blood sugar.
Medicines that lower blood sugar and appetite, used for diabetes and weight management.
An ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure.
A calcium channel blocker that lowers blood pressure.
An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that lowers blood pressure.
A beta blocker that slows heart rate and lowers blood pressure.
A diuretic (water pill) used to lower blood pressure.
Medicines that lower LDL cholesterol.
A blood thinner that needs regular blood tests to monitor.
Medicines that reduce blood clotting.
Thyroid hormone replacement for an underactive thyroid.
Medicines that reduce stomach acid production.
Medicines that neutralize or reduce stomach acid.
Medicines that treat bacterial infections; they do not work on viruses.
Medicines that relieve allergy symptoms.
Anti-inflammatory medicines that calm the immune system.
A fast-acting inhaled medicine that opens the airways.
Medicines that treat depression and some anxiety disorders.
Sedating medicines for anxiety or seizures; can be habit-forming.
Strong pain relievers that carry risks of dependence and overdose.
Medicines used for nerve pain and some seizures.
An emergency medicine for severe allergic reactions.
A preparation that trains the immune system to fight a specific disease.
The force of blood against artery walls, written as systolic over diastolic.
The amount of sugar in the blood.
A blood test showing average blood sugar over about three months.
Blood tests measuring cholesterol and triglycerides.
A blood test counting red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Blood tests that check kidney function, liver function, electrolytes, and glucose.
Blood tests that check how well the thyroid is working.
A test that records the heart's electrical activity.
An ultrasound of the heart.
An imaging test that uses radiation to view bones and some organs.
Detailed cross-sectional X-ray imaging of the body.
Imaging that uses magnets and radio waves to view soft tissues.
Imaging that uses sound waves to see inside the body.
A test of the urine for infection, blood, sugar, and more.
Removal of a small tissue sample for lab examination.
An X-ray screening test for breast cancer.
An exam of the colon with a camera to look for polyps or cancer.
A camera exam of the digestive tract.
A test that detects current infection with the COVID-19 virus.
A screening number based on height and weight.
The number of heartbeats per minute.
A procedure that treats a condition by operating on the body.
Surgery that replaces a damaged knee joint with an artificial one.
Surgery that replaces a damaged hip joint with an artificial one.
Surgery to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament in the knee.
A procedure that opens narrowed arteries, often placing a stent.
Surgery that reroutes blood around blocked heart arteries.
Treatment using exercise and movement to restore function.
A treatment that filters the blood when the kidneys cannot.
Drug treatment that kills fast-growing cancer cells.
Cancer treatment using high-energy radiation.
Emergency chest compressions and breaths when the heart stops.
Surgery to remove the appendix.
Surgery to remove the gallbladder.
Surgical delivery of a baby through the abdomen.
The muscular organ that pumps blood through the body.
The paired organs that exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Organs that filter waste from the blood and make urine.
A large organ that processes nutrients, medicines, and toxins.
A gland in the neck that controls metabolism through hormones.
An organ that makes digestive enzymes and insulin.
The joint between the thigh and the lower leg.
The column of bones that supports the back and protects the spinal cord.
A key ligament that stabilizes the knee.
The group of muscles and tendons that stabilize the shoulder.
